rows: Professional pesticide use should follow a suitable risk assessment and an integrated approach.
Only authorised products should be used for approved purposes and conditions.
Users should follow the product label and applicable code of practice.
Pesticides must be stored and transported securely and appropriately.
Handling and application should prevent unnecessary exposure to workers, bystanders and the environment.
Suitable equipment, PPE and hygiene controls may be required.
Application, storage and disposal records support legal compliance and incident investigation.
Spills, exposure or suspected misuse should be managed through appropriate emergency and reporting arrangements.
A pesticide authorisation or spray record does not prove correct application at a specific place and time.
Local conclusions require product, crop, rate, weather, equipment, operator, buffer and incident evidence.
Agricultural machinery contains moving parts capable of causing serious or fatal injury.
Machines should be suitable, properly guarded and maintained.
Operators must be trained, competent and authorised for the equipment.
Safe Stop should be used before clearing blockages, adjusting or maintaining machinery.
Power take-off shafts and other transmission parts require effective guarding.
People should be kept clear of danger zones and moving machinery.
Defeated or removed safety devices should be restored before use.
Machine selection and risk assessment should account for foreseeable misuse and operating conditions.
A machine model or guard shown in a photograph does not prove safe condition or use.
Risk conclusions require current guarding, isolation, competence, maintenance, task and operating-condition evidence.
MHRA publishes medicines recalls and notifications through the official alerts service.
Recall notices identify affected products, batches and the reason for action.
Recall classifications indicate the seriousness and urgency of the required response.
Healthcare organisations and supply-chain businesses should follow the actions stated in the notice.
Stock checks should use exact product and batch information.
Affected stock may need quarantine, return, replacement or other specified action.
Patient-facing action depends on the wording and risk assessment in the official notice.
Current alerts should be checked because recall status and advice can change.
A product name alone does not show that a particular pack or patient is affected by a recall.
Applicability requires the exact medicine, strength, presentation, batch, expiry, supplier and current notice.
MHRA publishes safety information for medical devices through the official alerts service.
Safety notices can concern device performance, use, maintenance, software or supply-chain issues.
Healthcare providers should identify affected devices using the notice's model, serial or lot information.
Actions may include inspection, software update, changed use, quarantine or removal from service.
Users should follow manufacturer and MHRA instructions stated in the notice.
Patient-risk assessment should reflect the device, clinical use and identified failure mode.
Completion of required actions should be recorded and verified.
Current device safety information should be monitored because advice can be updated.
A device category or brand does not prove that a specific unit is affected.
Unit-level conclusions require model, serial or lot, software, maintenance, clinical-use and notice evidence.
